title: Functions that move the plane
objectives: Picture a complex function as a map of the plane, using $z^2$ and $1/z$.

screens.prose: A complex function moves points: $w = z^2$ takes each $z$ on the left to $z^2$ on the right. The dashed circle is $|z| = 1$ and its image. Drag $z$ once round the circle and watch its image.

derive.caption: Angle of $z$: {{fixed(atan2(p1.y, p1.x) * 180 / pi, 0)}}°; angle of $z^2$: {{fixed(atan2(p1.v, p1.u) * 180 / pi, 0)}}°

screens.question: While $z$ goes once round the unit circle, how many times does $w = z^2$ go round?

options.why: You followed $z$ itself. Its image doubles every angle, so it moves twice as fast.
Squaring doubles angles, not halves them. When $z$ reaches 180 degrees, $z^2$ is back at 360.
Squaring doubles the angle once. Four turns would need $z^4$.

hints.text: Drag $z$ to 90 degrees, then to 180 degrees.
At 90 degrees the image is at 180; at 180 degrees it is back at 360.
Each turn of $z$ is two turns of $z^2$.

feedback.correct: $z = e^{i\theta}$ gives $z^2 = e^{2i\theta}$: the image turns twice as fast and goes round twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Drag $z$ to 90 degrees and read the angle of its image.

explain.text: On the unit circle $z = e^{i\theta}$, so $z^2 = e^{2i\theta}$: the angle doubles and the modulus stays 1. As $\theta$ runs from 0 to $2\pi$, $2\theta$ runs to $4\pi$, two full turns.

screens.prose: Two simple maps. $w = z + (1 + 2i)$ slides the whole plane. $w = (1 + i)z$ turns it by 45 degrees and stretches it by $\sqrt2 \approx 1.4142$, since $1 + i = \sqrt2\,e^{i\pi/4}$. The control switches between them.
screens.question: Where does $w = (1 + i)z$ send $2 + i$? Predict, then drag $z$ to $2 + i$ to check.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply $(1 + i)(2 + i)$ with $i^2 = -1$.

byKey.added: You added $1 + i$ to $2 + i$. That is a slide; the map multiplies.
byKey.i-plus: You used $i^2 = +1$. The product is $2 + 3i + i^2 = 1 + 3i$.

explain.text: $(1 + i)(2 + i) = 1 + 3i$. Its modulus $\sqrt{10}$ is $\sqrt5 \times \sqrt2$, and its angle is 45 degrees more than that of $2 + i$. The whole grid turns and stretches the same way.

screens.prose: A complex function is a **map** of the plane: each $z$ has an **image** $w = f(z)$. Each $z$ with $f(z) = w$ is a **preimage** of $w$. Here $w = z^2$ and the line $z = a + it$. The slider moves the line; its image is a parabola.
screens.question: Set $a = 1$. Drag $z$ to the point of the line whose image is $2i$.

hints.text: Points on the line are $1 + it$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Move along the line $\operatorname{Re} z = 1$ until the caption reads $2i$.

byKey.conj: That point is $1 - i$, whose square is $-2i$. Go above the axis.
byKey.p1: Stay on the line $\operatorname{Re} z = 1$ and read the caption.

explain.text: $(1 + it)^2 = (1 - t^2) + 2ti$, so $u = 1 - t^2$ and $v = 2t$: the parabola $u = 1 - v^2/4$. At $t = 1$ the image is $2i$. The points $t = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2$ land at $-3 - 4i$, $-2i$, $1$, $2i$, $-3 + 4i$.

screens.prose: Every $w \ne 0$ has two square roots, so $z^2$ gives it two preimages. Drag $z$ until the caption reads $f(z) = -3 + 4i$.
screens.question: Which $z$ in the upper half plane has $z^2 = -3 + 4i$?

hints.text: Its angle is about 126.9 degrees, so $z$ is at about 63.4 degrees.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Try $z = a + bi$ with $a^2 - b^2 = -3$ and $2ab = 4$.

byKey.other: $-1 - 2i$ is the other preimage, but it is below the real axis.
byKey.swapped: $(2 + i)^2 = 3 + 4i$. The real part needs $a^2 - b^2 = -3$, so $b$ is the larger.
byKey.conj: $(1 - 2i)^2 = -3 - 4i$: the imaginary part has the wrong sign.

explain.text: $a^2 - b^2 = -3$ and $2ab = 4$ give $a = 1$, $b = 2$ or $a = -1$, $b = -2$. So the preimages are $\pm(1 + 2i)$. $z$ and $-z$ always share an image, since $(-z)^2 = z^2$.

screens.prose: Now take the unit square with corners $0$, $1$, $1 + i$ and $i$. Under $w = z^2$ the corners go to $0$, $1$, $2i$ and $-1$.
screens.question: What does the image of the square look like?

options.text: A curved region: the segment from $-1$ to $1$ below, two parabolic arcs meeting at $2i$ above

options.why: You moved only the corners. The sides bend: the side $\operatorname{Re} z = 1$ becomes a parabola.
$z^2$ is not linear. It squares lengths and doubles angles, so straight sides curve.
Only 0 and 1 stay put. The corner $1 + i$ moves to $2i$.

hints.text: Follow one side of the square.
The side $1 + it$ maps to $(1 - t^2) + 2ti$, a parabola.
Two sides land on the real axis; two become arcs meeting at $2i$.

feedback.correct: Two sides fold onto the real axis and two bend into parabolas meeting at $2i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Track one side: $z = 1 + it$ maps to $(1 - t^2) + 2ti$.

explain.text: The bottom side $z = t$ goes to $[0, 1]$ and the left side $z = it$ to $[-1, 0]$. The sides $1 + it$ and $t + i$ become parabolic arcs from $1$ and $-1$ up to $2i$. The corner angles of 90 degrees at 0 open to 180, since $z^2$ doubles angles at 0.

screens.prose: Here are the four sides of the square and their images. The grid is off, because the engine draws it over the whole plane, not just the square.
screens.question: Drag $z$ to the corner of the square whose image is $-1$.

hints.text: Read the caption at each corner.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which corner squares to $-1$?

byKey.far: $1 + i$ squares to $2i$, the top of the image.

explain.text: $i^2 = -1$, so the corner $i$ lands at the left end of the image. The sides through $1 + i$ curve up to $2i$, and the image is the curved region from the last screen.

screens.prose: Now $w = 1/z$. It inverts the modulus and negates the argument, so $1/z = \bar z/|z|^2$. The circle $|z - 1| = 1$ is drawn with its image. The pole at 0 has no image, so that point is not drawn.
screens.question: What is $1/(1 + i)$?

hints.text: Drag $z$ to $1 + i$ on the circle and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $1 - i$.

byKey.conj: You took the conjugate and stopped. Divide by $|1 + i|^2 = 2$ as well.
byKey.no-conj: You halved but kept $+i$. The argument flips sign: $\bar z/|z|^2$.

explain.text: $1/(1 + i) = (1 - i)/2 = 0.5 - 0.5i$. The circle through 0 maps to a line: $z = 2 \mapsto \frac12$ and $z = 1 + i \mapsto \frac12 - \frac12 i$, both on $\operatorname{Re} w = \frac12$.

screens.prose: A colleague says $1/z$ is just the conjugate: after all, $1/i = -i = \bar i$. Drag $z$ to $2$ and compare.
screens.question: When does $1/z = \bar z$?

options.why: At $z = 2$, $1/z = 0.5$ but $\bar z = 2$. They agree only when $|z|^2 = 1$.
On the unit circle $z\bar z = 1$, so $1/z = \bar z$ there: $1/i = -i$.

hints.text: Drag $z$ to 2 and read both values.
$1/z = \bar z/|z|^2$, so they match only on $|z| = 1$.

feedback.correct: $1/z = \bar z/|z|^2$, which is $\bar z$ exactly when $|z| = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare $1/z$ and $\bar z$ at $z = 2$, then at $z = i$.

byKey.b: You checked a point on the unit circle only. At $z = 2$ the two differ: $0.5$ against $2$.

explain.text: $1/z = \bar z/|z|^2$, so the two agree only when $|z|^2 = 1$. Off the circle $1/z$ also rescales: $z = 2$ goes to $0.5$, not 2. The point $z = 0$ has no image; it goes to the point at infinity.

screens.prose: In code a map is a Python function. Write `map_points(f, zs)` returning the image of every point as a complex number. Write `square_roots(w)` returning both square roots: `cmath.sqrt(w)` first, then its negative.
screens.question: Complete `map_points` and `square_roots`.

widget.starter:
import cmath


def map_points(f, zs):
    out = []
    # append the image f(z) of every z
    return out


def square_roots(w):
    r = cmath.sqrt(w)
    return [r]

examples.call: map_points(lambda z: z * z, [1 + t * 1j for t in range(-2, 3)])

tests.call: map_points(lambda z: z * z, [1 + t * 1j for t in range(-2, 3)])
all(abs(w.real - (1 - w.imag ** 2 / 4)) < 1e-12 for w in map_points(lambda z: z * z, [1 + 0.1 * k * 1j for k in range(-25, 25)]))

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, one on 50 points of the line $\operatorname{Re} z = 1$. Lists are compared point by point as complex numbers with `cmath.isclose` (relative 1e-9).

feedback.correct: The line $\operatorname{Re} z = 1$ lands on the parabola $u = 1 - v^2/4$, and $-3 + 4i$ has roots $\pm(1 + 2i)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 wants the five images in order. Append `f(z)` for each `z` in `zs`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 wants both roots of $-3 + 4i$: `[r, -r]` with `r = cmath.sqrt(w)`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. `f` is a function: call it as `f(z)`.

explain.text: `cmath.sqrt` returns the principal root, the one with positive real part (or on the positive imaginary axis). The other root is its negative, because $(-r)^2 = r^2$. The test on 50 points checks $u = 1 - v^2/4$ for each image.

screens.prose: Under Black-Scholes with $r = 5\%$ and $\sigma = 20\%$, the one-year log return is normal with mean $0.03$ and variance $0.2^2$. Its characteristic function is $\varphi(u) = e^{0.03iu - 0.02u^2}$. The map sends the real line $u \in [0, 10]$ into the unit disc. Drag $u$ along the real axis.
screens.question: What is $|\varphi(5)|$?

hints.text: Drag $u$ to 5 and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Only the real part of the exponent, $-0.02u^2$, sets the modulus.

byKey.angle: 0.15 is the angle, $0.03 \times 5$ rad. The modulus is $e^{-0.02 \times 25}$.
byKey.sign: You dropped the minus sign: $e^{+0.5}$. The modulus of a characteristic function never exceeds 1.

explain.text: $\varphi(5) = e^{-0.5}e^{0.15i}$: modulus 0.6065 at angle 0.15 rad. At $u = 10$ it is $e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$ at 0.3 rad, curling in towards 0. A pricing library checks $\varphi(0) = 1$ and $|\varphi(u)| \le 1$ on its grid before using $\varphi$; level 3 prices with it.

ideas: A complex function maps the plane: $z$ has image $f(z)$. The $z$ with $f(z) = w$ are the preimages of $w$.
$z^2$ squares moduli and doubles arguments. It wraps the plane round twice, bends lines into parabolas and gives each $w \ne 0$ two preimages.
$1/z = \bar z/|z|^2$ inverts the modulus and negates the argument; it has no value at 0.
summary.trap: $1/z$ is not $\bar z$ in general: at $z = 2$, $1/z = 0.5$. They agree only on $|z| = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. $z$ and $-z$ have the same square.

explain.text: $(-z)^2 = z^2$, so the other root is $-(1 + 2i) = -1 - 2i$. The two roots sit opposite each other through 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the modulus and double the angle.

byKey.doubled: You doubled $2i$ instead of squaring it.

explain.text: $2i$ has modulus 2 at 90 degrees, so $z^2$ has modulus 4 at 180 degrees: $-4$.

quiz.prose: The map $w = 1/z$ at one special point.
quiz.question: What does $1/z$ do at $z = 0$?

options.text: It has no value there; points near 0 go far away

options.why: $1/z = \bar z$ only on the unit circle, and 0 is not on it.

feedback.correct: $1/z$ is undefined at 0, a pole: we say it goes to the point at infinity.

explain.text: $|1/z| = 1/|z|$, which grows without bound as $z \to 0$. So 0 has no image; it is the map's pole. By contrast $z^2$ sends 0 to 0, its only preimage.

quiz.prose: Square every point of the upper half plane $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$.
quiz.question: What is the image?

options.text: The whole plane except the non-negative real axis

options.why: Squaring doubles angles: angles from 0 to 180 degrees become 0 to 360.
That would halve the angles. Squaring doubles them.
Angles $2\theta$ with $0 < \theta < \pi$ never equal 0, so the non-negative real axis is missed.

feedback.correct: Angles $\theta \in (0, \pi)$ double to $(0, 2\pi)$: every direction but the positive real one.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What happens to the angles?

explain.text: Points of the upper half plane have angles strictly between 0 and $\pi$. Doubling gives every angle strictly between 0 and $2\pi$, so the image misses only the ray $[0, \infty)$.
